title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about progressing at university: turning what you know about mindset, motivation and goals into things you actually do. By the end you will be able to apply a growth mindset to a setback, use self-belief and the right kind of motivation on a demanding task, and set goals that move your learning forward.

You are past the start of your studies now. The question is no longer what success means, but how to keep making progress when the work gets harder. That is what these three habits are for.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: apply a growth mindset when you meet a setback in your studies
use self-efficacy and learning-focused motivation to sustain effort on a demanding task
set mastery goals that move your learning forward.

title: In real academic practice
body: Progressing at university is built on these three habits working together. Every demanding module, every mark that disappoints, every stretch of work that feels too hard, is a place to apply a growth mindset, draw on self-belief and set a goal that pulls you forward. Build these now and they carry you through the rest of your degree.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, putting a growth mindset to work: applying it when something goes wrong. Second, motivation and self-belief that last: keeping going on a demanding task. Third, setting goals that move you forward. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can apply a growth mindset when I meet a setback in my studies.
I can use self-efficacy and learning-focused motivation to keep going on a demanding task.
I can set mastery goals that move my learning forward.

title: Orientation
body: You already know the three factors that drive excelling: mindset, motivation and the goals you set. This lesson takes the first of them into practice. A growth mindset is most useful at the moment it is hardest to hold on to, which is when something has gone wrong.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are past the stage of simply naming the fixed and growth mindsets. The aim now is to apply a growth mindset to a real setback, choosing how you respond rather than only recognising the idea. That is the step from knowing about mindset to using it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: compare a fixed-mindset and a growth-mindset response to a setback
analyse how a student turns a poor mark into a growth-mindset response
apply a growth-mindset response to a setback in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Research describes two mindsets (Yeager and Dweck, 2012). A fixed mindset treats ability as set: a poor mark means you are simply not good at this. A growth mindset treats ability as something you build: the same poor mark shows you what to work on next.

A mindset is not a mood. It is the story you tell yourself about why something went wrong, and that story shapes what you do next. Progressing depends on bringing the growth version of that story to the setbacks you meet.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent setback in your studies, such as a disappointing mark or a task that defeated you. What did you tell yourself about why it happened? What would a growth-mindset version of that story have been?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A growth mindset earns its place when you hit a setback. A fixed response reads a poor mark as proof of your limits; a growth response reads it as information about what to do next. You can now tell the two responses apart, recognise a growth approach in action, and choose one yourself. The next lesson keeps you going once you have decided to carry on.

title: Orientation
body: Deciding to keep going after a setback is one thing; actually sustaining the effort is another. This lesson is about what keeps you working when a task is demanding: your belief that you can do it, and the kind of motivation driving you.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not here to learn that motivation matters, which you already know. The aim is to tell apart two kinds of motivation and to build your self-belief for a specific hard task, so that you have something to draw on when the work stops being easy.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: compare performance motivation with learning motivation and how each sustains effort
analyse how one of the four routes builds self-efficacy, including seeking support
apply a route to build self-efficacy for a demanding task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Self-efficacy is your belief in your own capacity to complete a particular task or reach a specific goal (Bandura, 1977). It is task-specific: you can feel capable in a seminar and unsure about an exam. Research suggests it grows in four ways: succeeding at a hard task, seeing someone like you succeed, encouraging feedback, and keeping stress manageable.

Motivation comes in two broad kinds. Performance motivation is driven by the marks you receive. Learning motivation is driven by mastering the subject and developing yourself. Both can move you, but learning motivation tends to sustain effort when a task is hard and the marks are not yet in sight.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a demanding task ahead of you. What is motivating you to do it: the mark, the mastery, or both? Which of the four routes to self-efficacy could you use to feel more capable of it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: What keeps you going on hard work is self-belief and the right kind of motivation. Self-efficacy is your belief that you can do a specific task, and it grows through mastery, seeing others succeed, feedback and managing stress. Learning motivation sustains effort better than chasing marks alone. You can now tell the two motivations apart and build self-efficacy on purpose. The last lesson turns this into goals.

title: Orientation
body: A growth mindset and self-belief keep you working, but working towards what? This lesson is about goals: the difference between chasing a mark and building capability, and how to set a goal that actually moves your learning on.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You can already set yourself targets. The aim here is to tell two kinds of goal apart and to turn a vague aim into a specific, mastery-oriented goal, so that the goals you set pull your learning forward rather than just naming a number.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: tell a performance goal apart from a mastery goal
rephrase a vague aim into a specific, mastery-oriented goal
set a mastery goal for a task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Goals come in two kinds. A performance goal is specific and targeted, such as getting a certain mark in one assignment. A mastery goal is less specific and more far-reaching: it aims at developing a capability you will use again and again.

Both have a place, but mastery goals are the ones that move your learning forward, because they outlast a single piece of work. A vague aim like do better is neither. The skill is turning that vague aim into a mastery goal that is specific enough to act on.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look at a goal you have set yourself recently, even a loose one. Was it a performance goal, a mastery goal, or just a vague aim? How could you rephrase it so it moves your learning forward?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Goals come in two kinds: performance goals target a mark, while mastery goals build a capability that lasts beyond one task. A vague aim is neither until you make it specific. You can now tell the two apart, rephrase a loose aim into a mastery goal, and set one of your own. With mindset, motivation and goals all working, you are ready to keep progressing.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Progressing at university is no longer about knowing that mindset, motivation and goals matter; it is about using them. You can apply a growth mindset to a setback, reading a poor result as information rather than a verdict. You can build self-efficacy and draw on learning motivation to keep going on a demanding task. And you can set mastery goals that move your learning forward. Look back at the confidence check to see how far you have moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, these three habits are things you practise in every module. Each setback you meet with a growth response, each demanding task you sustain through self-belief, each mastery goal you set, is progress you are driving yourself. This is also what study and professional life reward: the capacity to keep going and keep developing when the work is hard.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced course in this pathway takes these habits into self-regulated learning and the graduate capital you build across your whole degree. Going wider: the same habits underpin Academic Writing, Reflective Practice and Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback, where you put them to work on real tasks.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Two responses to the same setback
body: Four setbacks every student meets. Each card shows the fixed-mindset response and the growth-mindset response side by side, so you can see what changes.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Information cards contrasting fixed and growth responses.

_items.title: A disappointing mark
_items.subtitle: Fixed, then growth
_items.text: Fixed response: I am just not good at this subject. Growth response: this mark shows me where my understanding broke down, so I know what to work on next.

_items.title: Hard feedback
_items.subtitle: Fixed, then growth
_items.text: Fixed response: the tutor thinks my work is weak, so there is no point trying. Growth response: the feedback is a map of what to improve, and improving is the whole point of feedback.

_items.title: A week that defeated you
_items.subtitle: Fixed, then growth
_items.text: Fixed response: I could not keep up, which proves I do not belong here. Growth response: this week was too much at once, so I will change how I plan the next one.

_items.title: A peer doing better
_items.subtitle: Fixed, then growth
_items.text: Fixed response: they are cleverer than me, so I cannot catch up. Growth response: they have found something that works, so I can ask them what it is and try it.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students get the same disappointing mark back on an essay they worked hard on.

{{learner-a}} reads the mark, decides the subject is just not a strength, and files the essay away without reading the comments. The effort felt wasted, so there seems little point revisiting it. Nothing changes before the next assignment. This is a fixed-mindset response: the mark is treated as a verdict on ability.

{{learner-b}} is just as disappointed, but reads the feedback carefully and notes two things that cost marks: a weak structure and thin use of evidence. {{learner-b}} turns these into two specific things to practise on the next essay. The mark still stings, but it has become useful. This is a growth-mindset response: the mark is treated as information about what to do next.

Both students got the same mark. Only {{learner-b}} let it move their learning forward.

title: Growth-mindset moves
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These moves turn a setback into something that moves you forward. Try them the next time something goes wrong.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I read the setback as information about what to do next, rather than a verdict on my ability?
Have I named one specific thing that went wrong, instead of a general 'I am not good at this'?
Have I turned that one thing into something I can practise?
Have I used the feedback rather than filing it away?
Have I asked what a peer who did well actually did?
Have I noticed when I am telling myself a fixed-mindset story?

title: Formative check: fixed versus growth response
displayTitle: Which response applies a growth mindset to a poor mark, rather than a fixed one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response applies a growth mindset to a poor mark?

_items.text: Treating the mark as proof that the subject is not a strength of yours.
_items.feedback: That reads the mark as a verdict on ability, which is the fixed-mindset response.

_items.text: Reading the feedback to find the specific things to work on next.
_items.feedback: Yes. Treating the mark as information about what to improve is the growth-mindset response.

_items.text: Filing the essay away because the effort felt wasted.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the work treats the mark as final, which is the fixed-mindset response.

_items.text: Deciding a cleverer peer will always be ahead of you.
_items.feedback: That treats ability as fixed rather than something you can build.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A growth response reads the mark as information about what to work on next.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the response that uses the mark to find what to improve.
_incorrect.final: A growth response reads the feedback for what to work on next. The others treat the mark as a verdict on fixed ability.

title: Formative check: recognising a growth approach
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's approach a growth-mindset one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's approach a growth-mindset one?

_items.text: They turned the feedback into specific things to practise on the next essay.
_items.feedback: Yes. Using the setback to plan what to improve is the growth mindset in action.

_items.text: They were less disappointed by the mark than the first student.
_items.feedback: Both students were disappointed; the difference was what they did next.

_items.text: They decided the subject was simply not their strength.
_items.feedback: That is the fixed-mindset response the first student gave.

_items.text: They filed the essay away without reading the comments.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the feedback is the fixed-mindset response, not a growth one.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student turned the feedback into specific things to practise, letting the mark move their learning forward.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID with the mark, beyond how they felt about it.
_incorrect.final: The second student was growth-minded because they turned the feedback into specific things to practise. The other options describe the fixed response or just a feeling.

title: Formative check: choosing a growth response
displayTitle: You have just had a setback on a demanding task in {{context}}. Which response shows the growth mindset this lesson describes?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response shows the growth mindset after a setback?

_items.text: Pick out one specific thing that went wrong and plan how to practise it.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, naming one thing to work on and acting on it is the growth response.

_items.text: Conclude that you are not cut out for {{context}} and ease off.
_items.feedback: That reads the setback as a verdict on ability, which is the fixed response.

_items.text: Put the task out of your mind and hope the next one goes better.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the task leaves nothing changed for next time.

_items.text: Decide the task was unfairly hard and nothing could be done.
_items.feedback: Blaming the task alone leaves you with no move to make next.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, picking one thing to work on and planning to practise it is the growth response.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the response that turns the setback into something specific you can act on.
_incorrect.final: The growth response in {{context}} is to name one thing that went wrong and plan to practise it. The others treat the setback as a verdict or avoid it.

definition: Your belief in your own capacity to do a particular task or reach a specific goal.
extendedDefinition: Self-efficacy is task-specific: you can feel capable about a seminar yet unsure about an exam. Research suggests it grows in four ways: succeeding at a hard task, seeing someone like you succeed, encouraging feedback, and keeping stress manageable.
example: A student low on confidence before a statistics test builds self-efficacy by first mastering one past question, then another.
title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The key idea: self-efficacy
body: Reveal the key term for this lesson and read how self-efficacy is built.
instruction: Select to reveal the definition, then read how self-efficacy is built.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students face the same demanding task: a statistics assignment neither feels ready for.

{{learner-a}} is driven mainly by the mark and has little belief in being able to do statistics. The first hard question confirms the fear, and {{learner-a}} concludes there is no point and hands in a thin attempt. Low self-belief and a focus on the mark alone made the task easy to abandon.

{{learner-b}} also finds it hard, but starts by mastering one worked question, then a second, building a sense of being able to do it. {{learner-b}} is driven by wanting to understand statistics, not just to pass, and asks a friend who found it difficult last year how they got through. Belief and learning motivation keep the effort going to the end.

Both students found the task hard. Only {{learner-b}} built the self-efficacy, and leaned on the motivation, needed to finish it well.

title: Building motivation and self-belief
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These moves build self-efficacy and keep the right motivation in view. Try them on your next demanding task.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I broken the task down so I can master one small part first?
Have I found someone like me who has done this, to see it is possible?
Have I sought feedback that tells me where I am already getting it right?
Have I done something to keep my stress at a manageable level?
Have I asked what I want to learn from this, not only what mark I want?
Have I noticed when chasing the mark alone is draining my effort?

title: Formative check: performance versus learning motivation
displayTitle: Which option shows learning motivation and is more likely to sustain effort on hard work?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option shows learning motivation that sustains effort?

_items.text: Working at a subject because you want to master it and develop yourself.
_items.feedback: Yes. Learning motivation is driven by mastery and development, not the mark alone.

_items.text: Working only to get a particular mark in the next assignment.
_items.feedback: Being driven by the mark is performance motivation.

_items.text: Doing just enough to stay ahead of your classmates' grades.
_items.feedback: Comparing grades is a performance focus, not a learning one.

_items.text: Choosing the easiest option so your average stays high.
_items.feedback: Protecting a mark is performance motivation, and it can hold your learning back.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Learning motivation is driven by mastery and development, which tends to sustain effort on hard work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about mastering the subject, rather than the mark.
_incorrect.final: Learning motivation is driven by mastering the subject and developing yourself. The others are all about the mark, which is performance motivation.

title: Formative check: building self-efficacy
displayTitle: In the worked example, how did the second student build self-efficacy for the statistics assignment?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How did the second student build self-efficacy?

_items.text: By mastering one worked question, then another, and asking someone who had struggled through it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Mastery experiences and seeing someone like you succeed are two of the four routes.

_items.text: By reminding themselves that the mark was all that mattered.
_items.feedback: Focusing on the mark alone did not build the first student's self-belief.

_items.text: By deciding statistics was simply not for them.
_items.feedback: That is the low-self-efficacy response the first student gave.

_items.text: By handing in a thin attempt to get it over with.
_items.feedback: Giving up early is what low self-efficacy led the first student to do.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Mastering small parts and seeing someone like them succeed built the second student's self-efficacy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the moves that gave the second student a sense of being able to do it.
_incorrect.final: The second student built self-efficacy by mastering one question then another, and by asking someone who had struggled through it. The others describe low self-belief.

title: Formative check: building self-efficacy for a task
displayTitle: You face a demanding task in {{context}} and doubt you can do it. Which move best builds your self-efficacy for it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move best builds self-efficacy for a demanding task?

_items.text: Master one small part of the task first, so you have early proof you can do it.
_items.feedback: Yes. A mastery experience on a small part is one of the strongest routes to self-efficacy in {{context}}.

_items.text: Tell yourself the whole task is beyond you and lower your effort.
_items.feedback: That lowers self-efficacy rather than building it.

_items.text: Compare yourself with the best student in the group.
_items.feedback: Comparing yourself with the strongest can knock your self-belief, not build it.

_items.text: Pile on pressure by leaving it all to the night before.
_items.feedback: High stress works against self-efficacy, which is built partly by keeping stress manageable.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, mastering one small part first gives you early proof you can do it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that gives you a small success to build on.
_incorrect.final: The strongest move in {{context}} is to master one small part first, a mastery experience. The others lower self-belief or raise stress.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: From a vague aim to a mastery goal
body: Setting a goal that moves your learning forward happens in stages. Step through each one to see a vague aim turn into a mastery goal.
instruction: Step through each stage to see how the goal takes shape.

_items.title: Start with the vague aim
_items.body: You begin with something loose, such as 'do better at essays'. It is a wish, not yet a goal, because there is nothing specific to act on.

_items.title: Make it specific
_items.body: Name what 'better' means in practice. For example, build essays around a clear argument rather than a list of points. Now there is something concrete to work on.

_items.title: Aim it at mastery, not just the mark
_items.body: Point the goal at a capability you will reuse, such as structuring an argument, rather than at one mark. That is what makes it a mastery goal.

_items.title: Set a checkpoint
_items.body: Decide how and when you will know it is working, such as reviewing your next two essays for a clear argument. The goal is now specific, mastery-focused and trackable.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students set themselves a goal at the start of a new module.

{{learner-a}} writes down a single aim: get at least 65 in the final essay. It is specific, but it is a performance goal fixed on one mark. When an early task does not count towards that essay, {{learner-a}} puts little into it, and the goal gives no guidance on how to actually improve.

{{learner-b}} starts with the same vague wish to do well, but rephrases it: get better at building an argument across a whole essay. That is a mastery goal, aimed at a capability rather than one mark. It guides every task on the module, counting or not, because each is a chance to practise the argument-building the goal names.

Both students set a goal. Only {{learner-b}}'s goal moved their learning forward across the whole module.

title: Setting a mastery goal
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These steps turn a vague aim into a mastery goal that moves your learning forward. Try them on a goal of your own.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I started from the vague aim and said what it means in practice?
Have I pointed the goal at a capability I will use again, not just one mark?
Have I made it specific enough to act on this week?
Have I checked it is a mastery goal rather than a performance goal?
Have I set a way to tell whether it is working?
Have I made sure it guides tasks that do not count, as well as those that do?

title: Formative check: performance versus mastery goal
displayTitle: Which of these is a mastery goal rather than a performance goal?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is a mastery goal rather than a performance goal?

_items.text: Get better at building an argument across a whole essay.
_items.feedback: Yes. Aiming at a reusable capability is a mastery goal.

_items.text: Score at least 65 in the final essay.
_items.feedback: A single target mark is a performance goal.

_items.text: Come top of the group in the next test.
_items.feedback: Beating others on one result is a performance goal.

_items.text: Get a higher mark than last time.
_items.feedback: A mark comparison is a performance goal, not a mastery one.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A mastery goal aims at a capability you will reuse, not a single mark.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the goal about building a lasting capability, rather than a mark.
_incorrect.final: A mastery goal aims at a capability, such as building an argument. The others all target a mark, which makes them performance goals.

title: Formative check: rephrasing a vague aim
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's goal move their learning forward where the first student's did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's goal move their learning forward?

_items.text: It aimed at a reusable capability, so it guided every task on the module.
_items.feedback: Yes. A mastery goal guides work beyond a single marked piece.

_items.text: It set a higher target mark than the first student's goal.
_items.feedback: A higher mark is still a performance goal fixed on one result.

_items.text: It was written down more neatly.
_items.feedback: How a goal is written does not make it a mastery goal.

_items.text: It focused only on the final essay that counted.
_items.feedback: Focusing on one marked piece is the limit of the first student's performance goal.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The mastery goal aimed at a capability, so it guided every task, counting or not.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what let the second goal guide work across the whole module.
_incorrect.final: The second goal moved learning forward because it aimed at a reusable capability and guided every task. The others stay fixed on a single mark.

title: Formative check: setting a mastery goal
displayTitle: You want to set a goal for a task in {{context}}. Which is a well-formed mastery goal?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is a well-formed mastery goal for a task?

_items.text: Build a specific capability you will reuse, with a way to tell it is improving.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, a mastery goal names a reusable capability and how you will track it.

_items.text: Simply aim to do better than last time.
_items.feedback: That is a vague mark comparison, not a mastery goal.

_items.text: Target one mark in one piece of assessment.
_items.feedback: A single target mark is a performance goal.

_items.text: Promise yourself you will work harder in general.
_items.feedback: Working harder in general is a vague aim, not yet a goal you can act on.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A mastery goal in {{context}} names a reusable capability and how you will know it is improving.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the goal that names a capability to build and a way to track it.
_incorrect.final: A well-formed mastery goal in {{context}} aims at a reusable capability with a way to track it. The others are vague aims or single-mark targets.

ariaQuestion: A disappointing mark: which is the growth-mindset response?

_items.text: Read the feedback for the specific things to work on next time.
_items.feedback: Yes. Treating the mark as information to act on is the growth response.

_items.text: Accept that the subject is not one of your strengths.
_items.feedback: That treats the mark as a verdict on fixed ability.

_items.text: Put the work aside, since the effort felt wasted.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the work leaves nothing changed for next time.

_items.text: Decide a cleverer peer will always be ahead.
_items.feedback: That treats ability as fixed rather than something you build.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A growth response reads the mark as information about what to improve.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the response that uses the mark to improve.

body: Which statement reflects a growth mindset rather than a fixed one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement reflects a growth mindset rather than a fixed one?

_items.text: Ability in a subject can be built through effort and the right practice.
_items.feedback: Yes. Treating ability as something you can build is the growth mindset.

_items.text: You are either good at a subject or you are not.
_items.feedback: Treating ability as fixed is the fixed mindset.

_items.text: A setback proves you have reached your limit.
_items.feedback: Reading a setback as a limit is the fixed mindset.

_items.text: Feedback mainly tells you how able you already are.
_items.feedback: A growth mindset treats feedback as a guide to improvement, not a verdict.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A growth mindset treats ability as something you can build.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the statement that treats ability as buildable.

body: A student works at a subject to master it, not just for the mark. This motivation is...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student works at a subject to master it, not just for the mark. This motivation is...

_items.text: learning motivation.
_items.feedback: Yes. Being driven by mastery is learning motivation.

_items.text: performance motivation.
_items.feedback: Performance motivation is driven by the mark, not mastery.

_items.text: a fixed mindset.
_items.feedback: This is about motivation, not mindset.

_items.text: low self-efficacy.
_items.feedback: Self-efficacy is belief in your capacity, not the reason you are studying.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Being driven by mastery is learning motivation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What is driving the student: the mark, or mastery?

body: Which is one of the four research-backed ways to build self-efficacy?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is one of the four research-backed ways to build self-efficacy?

_items.text: Succeeding at a challenging task, which gives you proof you can do it.
_items.feedback: Yes. A mastery experience is one of the four routes to self-efficacy.

_items.text: Avoiding any task that feels difficult.
_items.feedback: Avoidance gives you no success to build belief on.

_items.text: Raising your stress so you take the task seriously.
_items.feedback: Managing stress, not raising it, is one of the four routes.

_items.text: Comparing yourself with the strongest person in the room.
_items.feedback: Seeing someone like you succeed helps; comparing with the strongest can knock your belief.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Succeeding at a challenging task is a mastery experience, one of the four routes.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option gives you real proof that you can do it?

body: Which of these is a mastery goal?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these is a mastery goal?

_items.text: Get better at structuring an argument across an essay.
_items.feedback: Yes. Aiming at a reusable capability is a mastery goal.

_items.text: Score at least 70 in the next exam.
_items.feedback: A single target mark is a performance goal.

_items.text: Finish higher in the group than last term.
_items.feedback: Beating others on a result is a performance goal.

_items.text: Just do better than before.
_items.feedback: That is a vague aim, not yet a goal you can act on.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A mastery goal aims at a capability you will reuse.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which goal aims at a lasting capability rather than a mark?

body: You want to turn 'do better at seminars' into a goal that moves your learning forward. What should you do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to turn 'do better at seminars' into a goal that moves your learning forward. What should you do?

_items.text: Make it specific and aim it at a capability, such as contributing one reasoned point each week.
_items.feedback: Yes. A specific, mastery-focused goal guides what you actually do.

_items.text: Leave it as 'do better', so it stays flexible.
_items.feedback: A vague aim gives you nothing specific to act on.

_items.text: Change it to 'get a better seminar mark than last term'.
_items.feedback: That turns it into a performance goal fixed on a mark.

_items.text: Promise yourself to try harder in general.
_items.feedback: Trying harder in general is still a vague aim.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Making it specific and aimed at a capability turns a vague aim into a mastery goal.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option makes the aim specific and about a capability?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: how to meet a setback with a growth mindset, how to keep going through self-belief and the right motivation, and how to set goals that move your learning forward. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to have mastered all three separately. The aim is to see mindset, motivation and goals as one connected practice rather than three separate ideas, so that it keeps working for you across the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect a growth mindset, self-belief and learning motivation, and mastery goals as one practice
analyse how the three habits work together in a student's ongoing study
apply the three habits together to keep progressing in your {{context}} study beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Progressing at university is these three habits working as one. It is not three separate tricks you reach for one at a time. It is a single practice you run again and again: meet a setback with a growth mindset, keep going on self-belief and learning motivation, and aim that effort at a mastery goal. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the parts of that one practice.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, progressing means running these three habits together whenever the work gets hard, not reaching for one at a time. A setback becomes information, which feeds the self-belief and learning motivation to keep going, which you aim at a mastery goal. Across a term, those small rounds add up into steady progress.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a demanding stretch of study ahead of you this term. How could you bring a growth mindset, your self-belief and learning motivation, and a mastery goal together to get through it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Progressing is most useful as one continuing practice, not three separate tricks. You meet a setback with a growth mindset, keep going on self-belief and learning motivation, and aim that effort at a mastery goal, then carry it into the next task. It is the three working together, round after round, that moves your learning forward.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Progressing at university is these three habits working as one, not three separate tricks. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Meet setbacks
_items.body: Meet a setback or hard task by reading it as information about what to work on, not a verdict on your ability.

_items.title: Keep going
_items.body: Build your self-belief for the task and lean on learning motivation, so you keep going rather than give up.

_items.title: Aim at mastery
_items.body: Turn what you are learning into a specific mastery goal that moves your learning forward.

_items.title: Carry it forward
_items.body: Carry that goal into your next piece of work, then meet the next setback the same way. The practice keeps turning.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students meet the same hard module. One reads a poor early mark as proof they cannot do it, loses heart, and sets only a target mark to chase. The other reads the mark as information, builds confidence by mastering one part at a time, and sets a goal to build a lasting skill. By the end of term, the second student's work is far stronger, because the three habits worked together.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to keep progressing
body: Use these to keep the three habits working together, rather than treating each task as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: When something goes wrong, do I read it as information about what to work on, rather than a verdict on my ability?
Do I build my self-belief for a hard task, instead of waiting to feel ready?
Am I working to master the subject, not only to chase the mark?
Have I set a mastery goal that will outlast this one piece of work?
Do I carry what I learn into my next task, rather than starting each one fresh?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat mindset, motivation and goals as one connected practice rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it more useful to treat mindset, motivation and goals as one connected practice rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat mindset, motivation and goals as one connected practice rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because they feed each other: a growth response builds the self-belief and motivation to keep going, which you channel into a mastery goal that sets up the next round.
_items.feedback: Yes. Each habit feeds the next, so the effort pays off round after round.

_items.text: Because using all three at once means you never meet a setback again.
_items.feedback: Setbacks still happen. The habits change how you respond to them, not whether they occur.

_items.text: Because setting one mastery goal removes the need for mindset or motivation.
_items.feedback: A goal needs a growth response and motivation behind it, or it stalls at the first setback.

_items.text: Because three separate ideas always take more effort than one habit.
_items.feedback: It is not about less effort. Working them together means each one supports the others.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Each habit feeds the next, so running them together pays off across your studies.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain when the three habits feed into one another.

displayTitle: A student gets a poor mark on an early essay. They read the feedback as showing what to work on, build their confidence by improving one weak area at a time, and set a goal to get better at structuring an argument. By the end of term their essays are stronger. What does this show?
body: A student gets a poor mark on an early essay. They read the feedback as showing what to work on, build their confidence by improving one weak area at a time, and set a goal to get better at structuring an argument. By the end of term their essays are stronger. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student gets a poor mark on an early essay. They read the feedback as showing what to work on, build their confidence by improving one weak area at a time, and set a goal to get better at structuring an argument. By the end of term their essays are stronger. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three habits worked as one practice: a growth response, self-belief and learning motivation, and a mastery goal, each feeding the next across the term.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three ran together, round after round, and the work improved.

_items.text: That the first poor mark was a fair verdict on their ability.
_items.feedback: The point is the opposite: the student treated the mark as information, not a verdict.

_items.text: That only the final essay mark matters, not what came before it.
_items.feedback: What came before is the point. The habits across the term made the later work stronger.

_items.text: That setting a goal alone was enough, with no change in mindset or effort.
_items.feedback: The goal worked because a growth response and real effort sat behind it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A growth response, self-belief and motivation, and a mastery goal worked together over the term.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at everything the student did across the whole term, not just one part.

displayTitle: You want to use these three habits together to keep progressing in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats them as one continuing practice?
body: You want to use these three habits together to keep progressing in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats them as one continuing practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use these three habits together to keep progressing in your subject this term. Which plan best treats them as one continuing practice?

_items.text: When a task goes badly, read it as information, build your self-belief, work to master the subject, and set a mastery goal to carry into the next task.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three habits together, again and again, across the term.

_items.text: Wait until the end of term, then judge in one go whether your mindset, motivation and goals were right.
_items.feedback: A single look back at the end cannot change work you have already handed in.

_items.text: Pick whichever one of the three habits feels easiest, and ignore the other two.
_items.feedback: The habits work because they feed each other. Dropping two leaves the third unsupported.

_items.text: Focus only on the marks, and change nothing about how you respond to setbacks.
_items.feedback: Chasing marks alone is the performance trap. Progressing needs a growth response and a mastery goal too.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading a setback as information, building self-belief, and setting a mastery goal keeps all three turning together.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps the three habits working together, round after round.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which best describes how a growth mindset, self-efficacy with learning motivation, and mastery goals work together?
body: Which best describes how a growth mindset, self-efficacy with learning motivation, and mastery goals work together?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which best describes how a growth mindset, self-efficacy with learning motivation, and mastery goals work together?

_items.text: They form one continuing practice for progressing: a growth response feeds self-belief and motivation, which you channel into a mastery goal, and the goal sets up the next round.
_items.feedback: Yes. One connected practice, run again and again.

_items.text: They are three separate techniques, best used one at a time and never together.
_items.feedback: They work best together, each one supporting the others.

_items.text: They matter only in your final year, once the hard choices are behind you.
_items.feedback: They matter from the moment the work gets demanding, which is now.

_items.text: They only help students who are already doing well.
_items.feedback: They help wherever you are starting from, which is the point of a growth response.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
